fichas.title: Daylight: physical basics
fichas.summary: Introduces daylight requirements for permanently occupied rooms, the visible spectrum and its wavelengths, and the units used to describe illumination and daylight in interiors. The page also diagrams electromagnetic radiation and the seasons in the northern hemisphere.
uses: Provide sufficient daylight in permanently occupied rooms
Maintain a reasonable visual connection with the outside
Understand the visible spectrum and daylight measurements

Light, wavelength, colour, unit
Within the range of electromagnetic radiation, visible light is a
relatively small part, with wavelengths of approx. 380-780 nm --7
0. Light (daylight and artificial light) is the range of electromagnetic
radiation between ultra violet and infra red, which can be
processed by the eye. The colours of the spectrum in daylight all
have their wavelength, from violet with relatively short wavelength
to red with the longest wavelength. Daylight, which is experienced
by the human eye as white, contains all wavelengths. The analysis
of wavelengths is of significance for architectural design.

The position of the sun results from the latitude. On the 21/3 and

zenith angle at noon (a.= 180°) is 51°--7 p. 48g f). The elevation
angle of the sun above the horizon is then goo - 51 o = 3go.

fichas.title: Position of the sun: azimuth and elevation
fichas.summary: Explains the sun’s position using azimuth and elevation angles, and relates its apparent seasonal path to date, time and latitude. It gives cardinal azimuth bearings, solstice declinations, and example noon angles for London at latitude 51° north.
uses: Determine the sun’s position for a particular location and time of year
Assess solar orientation and elevation for daylight and sunlight design
